topics.title: How to say because, so and therefore in Chinese
topics.blurb: Chinese states cause and result with paired connectors, and unlike English it usually keeps both halves of the pair.

topics.title: How to say but, although and however in Chinese
topics.blurb: Where English drops one half ("although it hurt, I went"), Chinese normally keeps both: 虽然 … 但是 ….

topics.title: How to say if, only if and no matter what in Chinese
topics.blurb: Conditions in Chinese come as pairs too: the condition word opens the first clause, and 就 or 才 or 都 answers it in the second.

topics.title: How to say both, also and not only in Chinese
topics.blurb: Adding a second thing usually needs a marker before the verb — 也, 又, 都 — not just a comma.

topics.title: How to say first, then and when in Chinese
topics.blurb: Chinese puts time in order of what happened first, and marks the sequence explicitly with 先, 然后, 一…就.

topics.title: 了, 着 and 过: talking about completed and ongoing actions
topics.blurb: Chinese has no verb tenses. These particles mark whether an action is finished, still going, or has been experienced.

topics.title: Chinese complements: saying how well and with what result
topics.blurb: A complement rides behind the verb to say how the action turned out — how well, how much, whether it worked at all.

topics.title: 把 and 被: doing something to an object
topics.blurb: 把 moves the object in front of the verb to stress what happens to it; 被 flips it round to say who it happened to.

topics.title: Describing things in Chinese: 很, 太 and degree
topics.blurb: Chinese adjectives work as verbs — you don't need 是. But a bare adjective sounds like a comparison, so a degree word comes along.

topics.title: How to compare two things in Chinese
topics.blurb: 比 does the work that -er and more do in English, and the adjective never changes form.

topics.title: How to ask questions in Chinese
topics.blurb: Chinese doesn't reorder the sentence to ask something. You add 吗, repeat the verb, or drop in a question word where the answer would go.

topics.title: Want to, can, should: Chinese modal verbs
topics.blurb: 会, 能 and 可以 all become "can" in English but mean different things — learned skill, physical ability, permission.

topics.title: Saying where something is and what there is
topics.blurb: 在 marks location and comes before the verb, not after it — the opposite of English word order.

topics.title: Being polite in Chinese: 请, 吧 and softening
topics.blurb: Chinese softens requests with particles and set phrases rather than with conditional verb forms.
